title: Pressure-cooker brown rice
subtitle: Nutty, fully cooked brown rice in 22 minutes
excerpt: Brown rice cooked under pressure with the absorption method. No babysitting, no boiling over, consistently tender grains with the nutty flavour and texture that makes brown rice worth cooking.
sourceNotes: Brown rice retains its bran layer and germ, which gives it a nuttier flavour and more resistant texture than white rice. It requires about twice the cooking time of white rice. The pressure-cooker absorption method compresses stovetop cooking from 40 to 50 minutes to about 22 minutes under pressure.

recipe.freezeNotes: Cool and freeze in airtight bags for up to 3 months.
recipe.batchNotes: Cook a large batch; refrigerate for up to 4 days and use across the week in grain bowls, salads, and stir-fries.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Refrigerate cooked rice for up to 4 days. Cool rapidly and refrigerate within 1 hour of cooking.

content.text: Brown rice is a straightforward swap for white in many dishes but requires about twice the cooking time on the stovetop, 40 to 50 minutes rather than 20. The pressure cooker compresses this to 22 minutes and produces tender grains without the risk of the dry, chalky centre that stovetop brown rice produces when the timing is slightly off.
Brown rice needs a slightly higher water ratio than white, 1:1.5 rather than 1:1.25, because the bran layer absorbs more liquid. Use cold water and allow the full 10-minute natural release.
Rinsing brown rice is optional. The bran layer is intact and there is less surface starch than in white rice. A quick rinse removes any dust and slightly reduces cook time.

Put the rinsed brown rice in the pressure cooker. Add 450 ml of cold water (a 1:1.5 ratio) and salt. Stir once and seal the lid. Bring to high pressure. Cook at high pressure for 22 minutes. Allow a natural pressure release of 10 minutes. Quick-release any remaining pressure and open the lid.
Fluff the rice with a fork. It should be evenly cooked and slightly chewy, brown rice retains more texture than white and this is correct. Serve immediately or spread on a tray to cool if storing.

rows.symptom: The rice is hard or chalky in the centre
rows.fix: Return to high pressure with an additional 50 ml of water for 5 minutes. Always allow the full natural release.

rows.symptom: The rice is wet and mushy
rows.fix: Open the lid and fluff, excess moisture will steam off. Reduce to 1.4 parts water next time.

content.text: Brown rice is a meal-prep staple, its denser texture holds up better than white rice in cold grain bowls and salads, and it keeps for 4 days in the fridge. The pressure cooker makes it a realistic weekday option rather than a weekend project. Use it wherever white rice would go, allowing for the additional chewiness.
